extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, critics, and informed readers of drama and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and aesthetic criteria for composing and judging drama, comedy, and verse — focusing on unity, moral effect, character-individualization, verse-harmony, avoidance of cheap devices, and fidelity in translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of beauty to humanize satire
rubrics_metrics.description: A satirist (Hogarth example) should often introduce a beautiful figure among humorous deformities so that the beauty 'diffuses through all, and over each of the group, a spirit of reconciliation and human kindness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including tenderness amid ridicule blends compassion with laughter and 'prevents the instructive merriment ... from degenerating into the heart-poison of contempt or hatred.' Anti-pattern: satire that only provokes contempt without reconciling human feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic unity and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramas (French tragedies noted) must be 'consistent works of art, preserving a fitness in the parts, and a harmony in the whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether parts fit and contribute to an overall harmony. Even when the drama forms 'a nature of their own' (a particular style), it should maintain internal coherence rather than a loose sequence of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevating the audience's understanding and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic scenes should 'affect us indeed, but within the bounds of pleasure, and in union with the activity both of our understanding and imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to transport the mind toward 'a sense of its possible greatness' and implant 'the germs of that greatness' rather than stupefying the audience with mere sensation or maudlin pathos. Anti-pattern: works that stupefy into mere sensation or rely solely on cheap emotional manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of the universal in the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aristotle: the poet should achieve an 'involution of the universal in the individual' — clothe universal truth in particular, individual form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good dramatic/poetic characters embody general truths while remaining distinctive individuals. The universal should be present but not dominate consciousness; the individual form must be vivid and particularized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap topicality and mechanical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither comedy nor tragedy should rely on 'wry faces, accidents of jargon, slang phrases for the day' or mechanical stage tricks and spectacles to produce laughter or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject ephemeral, topical jokes, jargon, and over-reliance on spectacle (e.g., gunpowder explosions, sensory gimmicks). Preference should be given to timeless language, situation, and psychologically believable action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject sentimental morality that flatters vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern sentimental plays often present 'the best Christian morality' that flatters the audience without demanding sacrifice — 'just as much... which you can exercise without a single Christian virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid moralizing that reassures and flatters the audience's vices rather than challenging them. Moral content should require genuine virtue or sacrifice, not mere comfortable sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding vice by subverting natural causes and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic popularity may be gained by 'the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things' and by rewarding criminals or vice with sympathy and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve credible causal relations and moral consequences. Do not contrive plots that unduly reward immorality simply to gratify the audience's resentment or envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize language, situations, and passion dynamics over mere plot novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The true interest of tragedy is not merely the novelty of the story but 'the delightful language of the poet... the situations, the action and reaction of the passions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when stories are familiar, value the poet's idiom, the shaping of situations, and the interplay of passions. Anti-pattern: treating drama like a mere new-novel curiosity where only plot surprise matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-individualization to illustrate universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Class-characteristics should be 'so modified and particularized in each person of the Shakesperian Drama, that life itself does not excite more distinctly that sense of individuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render social types into distinct, memorable individuals so that general truths are illuminated through particular lives. Avoid flat type-characters that only represent abstract classes without individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony in blank verse and poetic cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonious verse consists in 'the apt arrangement of pauses and cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs,' not in 'the even flow' or prominence of single antithetic lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing blank verse, shape long-period cadences and paragraph-like sweeps; use line breaks and pauses to create sustained musical and rhetorical motion rather than seeking striking single lines at the expense of overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist producing drama that imitates private life merely to flatter
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern plays often represent 'fac-similes of their own mean selves' to wheedle applause by encouraging sympathy with ordinary, meaner aspects of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama should not simply mirror the audience's mediocre habits to flatter them; it should elevate or critically examine human nature rather than reassure the audience in self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and honesty in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations must be faithful: Klopstock criticizes an English prose translation of his MESSIAH for being bad, adding pages and omitting half the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting material not present in the original or omitting substantial portions; a good translation should strive for fidelity to the source's content and tone. Anti-pattern: loose renderings that alter scope or meaning.
